metaDescription: Which stick blenders make reliable mayonnaise: bell shape, foot design, low speed and jar fit compared across six models, with the method that works.
expertTake: The Braun MultiQuick 5 at 350W is the top pick for mayonnaise, because its bell shaped foot sits flat on the jar floor and draws oil in slowly. The Turelar 400W is the value pick, since two speeds and a plain stainless shaft are all an emulsion needs. Skip high-wattage, many-bladed sticks for this job, because speed breaks a mayonnaise rather than building it.
introParagraphs: Mayonnaise is an emulsion, a suspension of tiny oil droplets in egg and acid, and a hand blender makes it in under a minute if the geometry is right. The trick is not power. It is a blade that sits flat on the bottom of a narrow jar so the oil is drawn in at the rate the egg can absorb it.

That makes foot design and speed control the whole game. A wide bell, a low speed and a jar that fits the head closely decide success, while a bigger motor often decides failure. This guide ranks six sticks on how well they suit that one narrow, fussy task.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 5 350W dual speed with beaker and whisk
products.description:
The MultiQuick 5 is the cleanest fit for mayonnaise because of its bell. The foot is a floral bell shape with the blades inside it, and when you press it flat to the bottom of a jar it creates a small chamber where oil is pulled up into the blade a little at a time. That is the mechanism an emulsion needs: a slow, steady feed of oil into a fast-moving egg base.

Two speeds are an advantage here. You run the low speed while the oil is still floating, and the stick will not go faster than the egg can handle. The 350 watt motor is not the strongest in this guide, but an emulsion does not need strength. A beaker is included, and its narrow shape is close to the ideal jar for the one-minute method.

To make it, put the egg, acid and seasoning in the beaker, pour the oil on top, rest the head on the bottom and start. Wait until the cloud of mayonnaise forms, then lift slowly. Rinse the bell straight away, since egg and oil residue are tough to remove once they dry. This is the stick to buy if mayonnaise is your main reason for owning one.
products.bestFor: Cooks whose main goal is a reliable one-jar mayonnaise.
pros: Bell foot seals against the jar floor for a slow oil feed
Two speeds prevent over-fast blending
Included beaker suits the one-jar method
SplashControl keeps the oil in the jar
cons: No chopper or masher in the kit

products.name: KitchenAid KHBV53 variable speed hand blender, matte black
products.description:
The KHBV53 earns its place through the jar and the trigger. A blending jar with a lid comes in the box, so you make the mayonnaise in the vessel and store it in the same one with the lid on. The variable speed trigger lets you start at a whisper and increase only when the emulsion forms.

A four-point stainless blade cuts in more planes than a simple two-blade foot, which helps the egg and oil combine quickly once the emulsion starts. The patented removable pan guard comes off for jar work, and you should take it off, because a guard on the head can hold the oil back from the blade.

The trade-off is that the foot is not a tight bell, so the oil is not drawn in as slowly as on the Braun. You compensate by pouring the oil in slowly and lifting the stick in small steps. Wash the arm and jar immediately, because egg residue is stubborn, and let them dry before storing. It is a very good option if you want a jar you can fridge.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want to make and store mayonnaise in the same jar.
pros: Blending jar with a lid for storage
Variable trigger for a gentle start
Four-point blade combines quickly
Removable arm cleans easily
cons: Foot is less tightly shrouded than a bell
Pan guard must be removed for jar work

products.name: Cuisinart CSB-179 Smart Stick variable speed hand blender

specList.label: Kit
specList.value: 3 cup chopper and grinder, chef's whisk

products.description:
The Cuisinart Smart Stick has a 300 watt DC motor that holds torque at low speed, and that is exactly what an emulsion wants. The variable speed control sweeps from low to high, so you can begin barely turning and then add speed once the mixture thickens. The listing also adds a chef's whisk and a chopper.

The quiet motor is a bonus when you are pouring oil in a thin stream with one hand and holding the stick with the other. The 8 inch shaft clears a tall jar easily, and the stainless foot is easy to press flat. Compared with the Braun it lacks the shrouded bell, so the oil is fed in a little faster, which means you must pour more patiently.

It is also the pick for people who want other things from the same stick, such as chopping herbs for a garlic aioli or whisking cream. Clean it by detaching the shaft and rinsing under hot water. Egg and oil residue clings to a cold shaft, so use warm water and a drop of soap before you set it aside.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want smooth variable speed and a whisk for sauces.
pros: Variable speed from near zero upward
DC motor holds torque at low speed
Whisk and chopper for aioli and herbs
Detachable stainless shaft
cons: Foot is not a tight bell

products.name: Turelar 400W corded immersion blender, 2 speeds
products.description:
The Turelar is the cheapest stick here and the listing calls it an emulsifier. A 400 watt copper motor, two speeds and a pulse-activated sensor give it the simplicity mayonnaise needs. The pulse control is useful because you can tap the sensor to start a slow emulsion without committing to a full run.

Two speeds mean you can run the low one for the whole job. That is the correct technique: low speed from start to finish, lifting the stick slowly as the emulsion forms. The stainless shaft is easy to rinse, and there are no attachments to track.

Compared with the Braun it has no bell, so the head is flatter and the oil moves faster. Practise the method before you rely on it for a large batch. Wipe the head after each batch, rinse the shaft and store it upright. It is a fine pick for a cook who makes mayonnaise occasionally and wants to spend little.
products.bestFor: Occasional mayonnaise makers who want the lowest outlay.
pros: Lowest price tier in the group
Two-speed pulse control is simple
Stainless shaft rinses easily
Listed as an emulsifier
cons: No bell-shaped shroud on the foot
No jar or beaker in the box

products.name: Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 500W immersion blender, 12 speeds
products.description:
The Bonsenkitchen brings a 500 watt high-torque motor, twelve speeds and a four-piece kit that includes a food processor bowl. A splash-resistant design and a scratch-resistant stainless body round it out. For mayonnaise, the twelve speeds are the feature: you can start low and step up in small increments as the emulsion thickens.

The 500 watt motor is more than an emulsion needs, which means the low end of the dial is the only part you will use. A strong motor spins up quickly, so the risk is going too fast too soon. Keep it at the lowest steps until the mixture has set.

The food processor bowl is an interesting extra, since a processor can also make mayonnaise from a base of egg and oil with a slow trickle. Wash the pieces by hand after use because oil clings to plastic and dishwashers do not always remove it. Anyone who wants one kit to cover many jobs, with mayonnaise as just one of them, gets the most flexibility here.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a fine speed dial and a processor bowl too.
pros: Twelve speeds with a gentle low end
500W motor has reserve for other jobs
Splash-resistant design keeps oil in the jar
Food processor bowl in the kit
cons: Strong motor spins up fast on a small batch

products.name: MasterChef 400W stainless immersion blender stick
products.description:
The MasterChef is a plain 400 watt stainless stick that the listing describes as an emulsifier. It has no attachments and no dial, which makes it the simplest thing on the list. For a cook who wants to make mayonnaise and nothing else, that simplicity is a virtue.

Its foot is a standard design, so the technique matters more than on the Braun. Use a tall jar that just fits the head, put the oil on top and press the head flat to the bottom. Hold it still until the emulsion starts, then lift slowly. Because there is only one speed setting to worry about, you cannot make a speed mistake.

The cost is limited versatility. Rinse the shaft right after each use, because mayonnaise dries sticky, and wipe the head. It is a reasonable pick for people who want a tool with a familiar name and no extras to look after.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a no-frills stick for emulsions.
pros: Plain design with nothing to misuse
Stainless shaft
Listed for emulsifying
Low price tier
cons: Foot design is standard, not shrouded

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Braun MultiQuick 5 has a bell with the blades inside, which draws oil in slowly when pressed flat to the jar floor. A plain foot, like the MasterChef's, feeds oil faster and demands more patience. For repeatable mayonnaise the bell wins.

Mayonnaise forms at the bottom of the speed range. The Cuisinart CSB-179 sweeps from low, the KitchenAid KHBV53 uses a trigger and the Bonsenkitchen has twelve steps. A stick that starts fast breaks the emulsion before it forms.
A jar only a little wider than the head keeps the egg in contact with the blade. The KitchenAid includes a jar and the Braun a beaker. Use a tall, narrow vessel and press the head flat.
A 350W or 400W motor is plenty. The Bonsenkitchen's 500W is more than needed, so only use its lowest settings. Extra power adds the risk of splitting the emulsion.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Easy cleaning of egg and oil
buyingCriteria.explanation: Egg and oil dry into a sticky film. A detachable shaft, like the Cuisinart's, is easier to wash. Rinse with warm water straight after use.

Classic mayonnaise uses raw egg, so use fresh eggs, or pasteurised eggs if you serve the sauce to children, older adults or anyone who is pregnant. Refrigerate the finished mayonnaise and use it within a few days.

howWeEvaluated.title: Foot and bell geometry
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the Braun bell against the flatter feet on the others. A bell controls the oil feed. We treated geometry as the first criterion for this task.

howWeEvaluated.title: Low-speed behaviour
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how low each stick can run, from the two speeds of the Braun to the twelve steps of the Bonsenkitchen. An emulsion needs a gentle start. Owner feedback patterns on split mayonnaise shaped the weighting.

howWeEvaluated.title: Vessel fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered the jar or beaker that comes with each stick and how well the head fits a standard jar. The KitchenAid jar and the Braun beaker lead. Fit matters more than power.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleanup after egg and oil
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared detachable shafts and plain sticks. Mayonnaise residue is sticky and hard to remove once dry. Detachable parts score higher, and so does a head with few crevices where egg can lodge and go off.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value for one task
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered the six by relative price tier, with the Turelar 400W lowest and the KitchenAid KHBV53 mid-range. A stick bought mainly for mayonnaise should not cost much.

cards.label: Bell foot
cards.text: The Braun MultiQuick 5 draws oil in slowly and forgives a quick pour. It suits cooks who want the sauce to come together on the first try.

cards.label: Flat foot
cards.text: The MasterChef and Turelar rely on your technique. They suit cooks who are willing to pour slowly and lift in small steps.

howToChoose.note: Choose a bell if you want forgiveness, a flat foot if you will practise.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A head that sits flat on the jar floor, a low speed and a jar just wider than the head. Put the egg at the bottom and the oil on top.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Braun MultiQuick 5 with its beaker and bell is the closest match to that method.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want a jar you can store in the fridge, as with the KitchenAid KHBV53, or a processor bowl, as with the Bonsenkitchen.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You make mayonnaise a few times a year. The Turelar 400W is enough.

maintenance.task: Rinse egg and oil off at once
maintenance.why: Dried egg and oil form a sticky film. Warm water and a drop of soap clear it easily while it is fresh.
Oil clings to plastic and can go rancid. Hot soapy water removes it.

A dent in the bell lets oil escape and weakens the emulsion. Check for dents or cracks, because even a small deformation changes how the head seals to the jar floor and how oil is drawn into the blade.
Oil splash makes grips slippery. A damp cloth with a little soap removes it.
Damp shafts grow odors. Dry fully before storing.

faq.q: Can an immersion blender make mayonnaise?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of the easiest ways. Put the egg, acid and seasoning in a tall jar, pour the oil on top, rest the head on the bottom and start. Lift slowly once the emulsion forms.

The oil was fed in too fast or the stick ran too fast. Start again with a fresh egg yolk and add the split mixture slowly. Cold ingredients are another common cause, so let the egg and acid reach room temperature before you begin, and keep the jar steady on the counter.

faq.q: Do I need a high-wattage stick?
faq.a: No. A 350W to 400W motor is enough. Speed control and foot design matter more. An overpowered stick spins up in an instant, and mayonnaise forms best when the blade starts slowly and builds.
Use fresh eggs, or pasteurised eggs if you serve children, older adults or anyone who is pregnant. Refrigerate the sauce and use it within a few days.

A neutral oil such as sunflower or light olive oil works well. Strong extra virgin olive oil can taste bitter when blended, because the blades release compounds that stay muted in a whisked sauce. Many cooks use a neutral oil for most of the volume and finish with a spoonful of olive oil.

faq.q: Can I make aioli the same way?
faq.a: Yes. Add crushed garlic to the jar with the egg. The method is identical, though the garlic needs to be finely crushed or grated first, since whole pieces can catch under the head and stop the emulsion from forming.
